nodes.name: Roe's theorem
nodes.statement:
Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of real-valued functions of a real variable with
	$\frac{d}{dx}f_{k}=f_{k+1}.$ In 1980, J. Roe \cite{R} proved that
	if there exists a constant $M>0$ such that $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M\text{ for all }n\text{ and }x$
	then $f_{0}(x)=a\sin(x+\theta)$ for some $a,\theta\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: A doubly infinite sequence of uniformly bounded functions with $f_k'=f_{k+1}$ has $f_0=a\sin(x+\theta)$.
assumptions: there exists a constant $M>0$ such that $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M\text{ for all }n\text{ and }x$

nodes.name: Strichartz's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfying $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{k}=f_{k+1}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where $M$ is a real number. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{0}=-f_{0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniformly bounded doubly infinite sequences with $\Delta f_k=f_{k+1}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ force $f_0$ to be an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $-1$.
assumptions: $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfying $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{k}=f_{k+1}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$
$|f_{k}(x)|\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where $M$ is a real number
nodes.label: th2

nodes.name: homogeneous tree
nodes.statement: A homogeneous tree $\mathfrak{X}$ of degree $q+1$ is a connected graph with no loops such that every vertex is adjacent to $q+1$ other vertices.
differentia: every vertex is adjacent to $q+1$ other vertices

nodes.name: degree assumption q >= 2
nodes.statement: Henceforth we assume $q\geq 2$.

nodes.name: distance on the tree
nodes.statement: The distance $d(x,y)$ between two vertices $x$ and $y$  defined as the number of edges joining $x$ and $y$.

nodes.name: Laplace operator on a homogeneous tree
nodes.statement:
The natural Laplace operator (or Laplacian) $\mathcal L$ on $\mathfrak X$ is defined by
\begin{equation} \mathcal Lf(x)=f(x)-\frac{1}{q+1}\sum\limits_{y:d(x,y)=1}f(y).\end{equation}

nodes.name: Laplacian formula
nodes.statement: \mathcal Lf(x)=f(x)-\frac{1}{q+1}\sum\limits_{y:d(x,y)=1}f(y).
nodes.label: eq00

nodes.name: spherical function and eigenvalue map gamma
nodes.statement_short: $\phi_z$ is the radial eigenfunction of $\mathcal L$ with eigenvalue $\gamma(z)=1-(q^{1/2+iz}+q^{1/2-iz})/(q+1)$.

nodes.name: Counterexample to Strichartz's theorem on homogeneous trees
nodes.statement: Note that the image of $S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$ under the map $\gamma$ is an elliptic region which intersects $\{w\in\mathbb{C}:|w|=1\}$ in infinitely many points. Assume $f_{k}(x)=\gamma(z_{1})^{k}\phi_{z_1}(x)+\gamma(z_{2})^{k}\phi_{z_2}(x)$ for some $z_1,z_2$ in $S_1$ such that $\gamma(z_1)\neq\gamma(z_2)$ and $|\gamma(z_1)|=|\gamma(z_2)|=1$. Since $\phi_z$ is uniformly bounded on $S_1$, $\{f_k\}$ satisfy all the hypothesis of the Theorem \ref{th2}, but  $f_{0}$ fails to be an eigenfunction of $\mathcal{L}$.
nodes.statement_short: A sum of two bounded spherical functions with distinct unimodular eigenvalues satisfies Strichartz's hypotheses but is not an eigenfunction.

nodes.name: Theorem A
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $z\in\mathbb R\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$. If there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ then $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$. In particular, there exists $F\in L^{2}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$.
nodes.statement_short: Weak-$L^2$ bounds $\|\mathcal L^k f\|\le M|\gamma(z)|^k$ for all $k\in\mathbb Z$ with real $z\notin(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$ force $f$ to be a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction (a Poisson transform).
assumptions: there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.label: Theorem A

nodes.name: Theorem B
nodes.statement_short: For $1<p<2$ and $z$ on the boundary of $S_p$ at $n\tau$ (resp. $(2n+1)\tau/2$), weak-$L^{p'}$ bounds on positive (resp. negative) powers of $\mathcal L$ force $f$ to be an eigenfunction.
assumptions: there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{-k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{-k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{-k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{-k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$

nodes.label: Theorem B

nodes.name: Theorem A as an extension of Strichartz's result
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma(z)\in \mathbb R$ whenever $z\in\mathbb R\setminus(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$, Theorem A can be thought of as a suitable extension of  Strichartz's result on homogeneous tree.  In particular if we define $f_{k}=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal{L}^{k}f$, then the statement of Theorem A resembles Theorem \ref{th2} with the only difference that the $L^{\infty}$ boundedness is being replaced by weak $L^{2}$ boundedness.

nodes.name: Poisson representation of weak L^p eigenfunctions
nodes.statement: It was proved in \cite{KR} that any weak $L^p$ eigenfunction of the Laplacian of $\mathfrak{X}$ can be represented by the Poisson transform of a $L^{p}$ function on the boundary.
assumptions: any weak $L^p$ eigenfunction of the Laplacian of $\mathfrak{X}$
conclusions: can be represented by the Poisson transform of a $L^{p}$ function on the boundary

nodes.name: number systems notation
nodes.statement: The letters $\mathbb{Z}_{+},\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ will respectively denote the set of all non-negative integers, integers, real numbers and complex numbers.

nodes.name: real and imaginary part notation
nodes.statement: For $z\in \mathbb C$ we use the notation $\mbox{Re } z$ and $\Im z$ for real and imaginary part of $z$ respectively.

nodes.name: isometry group G and stabilizer K
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be the group of isometries of the metric space $(\mathfrak X,d)$ and let $K$ be the stabilizer of $o$ in $G$.

nodes.name: radial function space notation
nodes.statement: If $E(\mathfrak X)$ is a function space on $\mathfrak X$  we will denote by $E(\mathfrak X)^\#$  the radial functions in $E(\mathfrak X)$.

nodes.name: infinite geodesic ray
nodes.statement: An infinite geodesic ray $\omega$ in $\mathfrak X$ is an one-sided sequence $\{\omega_{n}: n=0,1,2\ldots \}$ where $\omega_n$'s are in $\mathfrak X$.

nodes.name: reference point o
nodes.statement: Let $o$ be some arbitrarily fixed point in $\mathfrak X$.

nodes.name: boundary of the tree
nodes.statement: The boundary of $\mathfrak X$ is the set of all infinite geodesic rays starting at $o$ and will be denoted by $\Omega$.
nodes.genus: set of all infinite geodesic rays

nodes.name: quasi-invariant boundary measure
nodes.statement: Let $\nu$ be the $G$-quasi-invariant probability measure on the boundary $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Poisson kernel
nodes.statement:
The Poisson kernel $p(g\cdot o,\omega)$ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative $d\nu(g^{-1}\omega)/d\nu(\omega)$ and explicitly written as
$$ p(x,\omega)=q^{h_{\omega}(x)} \;\; \forall x\in \mathfrak X \;\; \forall \omega\in\Omega,$$
where $h_{\omega}(x)$ is the height of $x$ in $\mathfrak X$ with respect to $\omega$ (see \cite{FTC} for details).
nodes.statement_short: The Poisson kernel is $p(x,\omega)=q^{h_\omega(x)}$, the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the boundary measure, with $h_\omega$ the height.

nodes.name: Poisson transform
nodes.statement:
The Poisson transformation $\mathcal{P}_{z}:C(\Omega)\rightarrow C(\mathfrak X)$ is given by the formula
$$\mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x)=\int\limits_{\Omega}p^{1/2+iz}(x,\omega)\eta(\omega)d\nu(\omega).$$

nodes.name: period tau
nodes.statement: It is obvious that $\mathcal{P}_{z}=\mathcal{P}_{z+\tau}$, where $\tau=2\pi/\log q$.

nodes.name: torus T
nodes.statement: We denote the torus $\mathbb R/\tau \mathbb Z$ by $\mathbb{T}$, which can be identified with the interval $[-\tau/2,\tau/2)$.

nodes.name: Poisson transforms are eigenfunctions of the Laplacian
nodes.statement: It is a well-known fact that $\mathcal L \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x) =\gamma(z) \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x)$ for every $z$ in $\mathbb{C},$ where expression of $\gamma(z)$ is given in (\ref{eq01}).

nodes.name: elementary spherical function
nodes.statement: The elementary spherical function $\phi_z$ on $\mathfrak X$ is the Poisson transform of the constant function $\mathbf{1}$.

nodes.name: radialization
nodes.statement:
For a suitable function $f$ on $\mathfrak{X}$, its radialization $\varepsilon f$ is defined as
\begin{equation} \varepsilon f(x)=\int\limits_{K}f(k\cdot x)dk,
\end{equation}
where $dk$ is the normalized measure on $K$.

nodes.name: radialization formula
nodes.statement: \varepsilon f(x)=\int\limits_{K}f(k\cdot x)dk,
nodes.label: Equation 2.3

nodes.name: properties of radialization
conclusions: The operator  $\varepsilon$  commutes with the Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$, that is $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon f)=\varepsilon(\mathcal{L}f).$
Also if $\mathcal L u=\gamma(z)u$ then $\varepsilon u (x)=u(o)\phi_z(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Radialization contracts Lorentz norms, commutes with $\mathcal L$, and maps a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction $u$ to $u(o)\phi_z$.

nodes.name: explicit formula for the spherical function
nodes.statement_short: Closed form of $\phi_z$ via the meromorphic $\mathbf c$-function, with the degenerate cases $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$.

nodes.name: spherical function formula
nodes.label: eqsf

nodes.name: spherical functions bounded on S_1
nodes.statement: It is easy to verify that $|\phi_{z}(x)|\leq 1$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$ whenever $z\in S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$.

nodes.name: delta_p and strip S_p
nodes.statement:
For $p\in(1,\infty)$ we define
$$\delta_p=\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\;\;\; \text{and}\;\;\; S_p=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq|\delta_p|\}.$$

nodes.name: convention delta_1
nodes.statement: We assume $\delta_1=-\delta_\infty=1/2$ so that $S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$.

nodes.name: interior and boundary of S_p
nodes.statement: We shall henceforth write $S_p^\circ$ and $\partial{S_p}$ to denote the usual interior and boundary of $S_p$ respectively.

nodes.name: Derivation of the norm estimates of phi_z
nodes.statement: The following norm estimates of $\phi_{z}$ can be derived by using  (\ref{eqsf}) (see \cite{FTP1} for details).
nodes.statement_short: Derived from the explicit formula for $\phi_z$ (details in the cited work).

nodes.name: Lorentz-space membership of spherical functions
nodes.statement_short: $\phi_z\in L^{p'}$ iff $z\in S_p^\circ$, $\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}$ iff $z\in S_p$, and the $L^{2,\infty}$ case depends on $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb Z$.
conclusions: $\phi_z\in L^{p'}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p^\circ$
$\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p.$
$\phi_z\in L^{p'}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p^\circ$
$\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}(\mathfrak X)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p.$

nodes.label: phiz

nodes.name: gamma(S_p interior) in the point spectrum
nodes.statement: From the above lemma it is clear that $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum of the $\mathcal L,$ which is a bounded operator on $L^{p^\prime}(\mathfrak X)$.
conclusions: $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum of the $\mathcal L,$

nodes.name: L^p-spectrum of the Laplacian on homogeneous trees
nodes.statement_short: The $L^p$-spectrum of $\mathcal L$ is $\gamma(S_p)$, an elliptic region, degenerating for $p=2$ to $[1-b,1+b]$.
conclusions: the $L^{p}$-spectrum $\sigma_{p}(\mathcal{L})$ of $\mathcal{L}$ is the image of $S_p$ under the map $\gamma$

nodes.name: elliptic L^p spectrum region
nodes.statement: \left[\frac{1-\mbox{Re }(w)}{b\cosh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}+\left[\frac{\Im(w)}{b\sinh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}\leq 1,\text{ where }b=\frac{2\sqrt{q}}{q+1}.
nodes.label: equation 1.2

nodes.name: spherical Fourier transform
spherical Fourier transform formula
nodes.statement: \hat{f}(z)=\sum\limits_{x\in\mathfrak X}f(x)\phi_z(x)\quad\text{ where }z\in\mathbb C.
nodes.label: Equation 2.6

nodes.name: spherical transform is even and periodic
nodes.statement: The symmetric properties of the spherical function implies that $\hat{f}$ is even and $\tau$-periodic on $\mathbb{C}$.

nodes.name: p-Schwartz space
p-Schwartz seminorms
nodes.statement: \nu_{m}(f)=\sup\limits_{x\in\mathfrak{X}}(1+|x|)^{m}q^{|x|/p}|f(x)|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}.
nodes.label: Equation 2.7

nodes.name: p-Schwartz spaces are Frechet
nodes.statement: It is known that $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ form Fr\'{e}chet space with respect to these countable seminorms $\nu_{m}(\cdot)$ and are also known as the $p$-Schwartz spaces of rapidly decreasing functions on $\mathfrak{X}$ (see \cite{CMS}).
conclusions: $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ form Fr\'{e}chet space with respect to these countable seminorms $\nu_{m}(\cdot)$

nodes.name: space H(S_p)^#
nodes.statement_short: Even $\tau$-periodic functions on $S_p$, holomorphic inside, continuous on the boundary, with all derivatives bounded (seminorms $\mu_m$).

nodes.name: seminorms mu_m
nodes.statement: \mu_{m}(g)=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^m}{dz}g(z)\right|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}.
nodes.label: Equation 2.8

nodes.name: Betori-Faraut-Pagliacci isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: It was  proved in \cite{JF} that the spherical Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$.
conclusions: the spherical Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$

nodes.name: L^p-tempered distribution
nodes.statement: For $1<p\leq 2$, a linear functional $T:\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is said to be a $L^{p}$-tempered distribution if $\langle T,f_{n}\rangle\rightarrow 0$ whenever $\nu_{m}(f_{n})\rightarrow 0$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: radial distribution
nodes.statement:
The distribution $T$ is said to be radial if
$$\langle T,f\rangle=\langle T,\varepsilon f\rangle,\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X}).$$

nodes.name: radial part of a distribution
nodes.statement:
In fact the radial part of an $L^{p}$-tempered distribution $T$ is again an $L^{p}$-tempered distribution defined by
$$\langle\varepsilon T,f\rangle=\langle T,\varepsilon f\rangle,\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X}).$$

nodes.name: left translation of a distribution
nodes.statement:
The left translation $\tau_{x}$ of $T$ by an element $x\in G$ is defined as follow if $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ then
$$\langle \tau_{x}T,f\rangle=T(\tau_{x^{-1}}f)=T\ast f^{\ast}(x^{-1})$$
where $f^{\ast}(x)=f(x^{-1})$.

nodes.name: spherical Fourier transform of a radial distribution
nodes.statement:
Finally, the spherical Fourier transform $\hat{T}$ of a radial $L^{p}$-tempered distribution $T$ is a linear functional on $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ defined by the following rule:
$$\langle \hat{T},\psi\rangle=\langle T,f\rangle,\text{ where }\psi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}\text{ and }\hat{f}=\psi.$$

nodes.name: Lemma A
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: A bounded sequence of $L^2$-tempered distributions with $\mathcal LT_k=z_0T_{k+1}$ gives an eigendistribution if $|z_0|$ lies in the $L^2$-spectrum, and vanishes otherwise.
assumptions: $\{T_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of $L^2$-tempered distributions on $\mathfrak{X}$
$|\langle T_k,\phi\rangle|\leq M\nu(\phi)$ for all $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})$, where $\nu$ is some fixed semi-norm of $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})$ and $M>0$
nodes.label: Theorem10

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A
nodes.statement:
We first prove part (a) of the theorem with an additional assumption that the distributions $T_{k}$ are radial.
Fix $z_{0}\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z_{0}|\in[1-b,1+b]$. Then $z_{0}=\gamma(\alpha)e^{i\theta}$ for a unique $\alpha\in[0,\tau/2]$ where $\theta=\arg z_{0}$.
It follows from hypothesis (1) of the theorem that $\mathcal{L}^{k}T_{0}=e^{ik\theta}\gamma(\alpha)^{k}T_{k}$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. This implies
\begin{equation} \widehat{T_{0}}=e^{ik\theta}\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\widehat{T_{k}}.
\end{equation}
 Let $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ be such that $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\tau/2,-\alpha-r]\cup[\alpha+r,\tau/2]$ where $r>0$. Observing the fact that $\gamma(\alpha)^{k}/\gamma(\cdot)^{k}\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ and using hypothesis (2) of the theorem, we have

$$|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|=\left|\left\langle\widehat{T_{k}},e^{ik\theta}\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right\rangle\right|=\left|\left\langle T_{k},\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right\rangle\right|
	\leq M\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right].$$

By the isomorphism theorem \ref{lp isom}, there exists  a fixed seminorm $\mu$ on $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ such that
$$\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right]
	\leq C\mu\left[\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right]=\sup\limits_{\alpha+r\leq|s|\leq\tau/2}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)\right|\rightarrow 0\text{ as }k\rightarrow\infty.$$
 By similar argument as above and letting $k\rightarrow -\infty$, we can show that $\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle=0$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\alpha+r,\alpha-r]$. We proved that for any $r>0$ and for every $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ such that $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\tau/2,-\alpha-r]\cup[-\alpha+r,\alpha-r]\cup[\alpha+r,\tau/2]$, $\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle=0$.

We now show that
\begin{equation} (\mathcal{L}-\gamma(\alpha))^{N+1}T_{0}=0\quad\text{for some }N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}
\end{equation}
In view of the fact that the spherical transform is an isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$, it is enough to prove that
\begin{equation} (\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}}=0\quad\text{for some }N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.
\end{equation}


Let $g$ be an infinitely differentiable even function on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $g\equiv 1$ on $[-1/2,1/2]$ and $\mbox{supp}(g)\subseteq(-1,1)$. Define
$$\psi_{\epsilon}(s)=\begin{cases}
g((s-\alpha)/\epsilon) & s\in[0,\tau/2]\\
g((-s-\alpha)/\epsilon) & s\in[-\tau/2,0].
\end{cases}
$$
Here $\epsilon$ is suitably chosen positive number such that $\psi_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with $\mbox{supp}(\psi_{\epsilon})\subseteq(-\alpha-\epsilon,-\alpha+\epsilon)\cup(\alpha-\epsilon,\alpha+\epsilon)$.

Note that if $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$, then $(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(\cdot))^{N+1}\phi(1-\psi_{\epsilon})\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with its support inside $[-\tau/2,-\alpha-\epsilon/2]\cup[-\alpha+\epsilon/2,\alpha-\epsilon/2]\cup[\alpha+\epsilon/2,\tau/2]$. and using the result proved in step 1, we have
\begin{align}
	|\langle(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|	 &\leq|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(1-\psi_{\epsilon})\rangle|+|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\rangle|\nonumber\\
	&=|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\rangle|\nonumber\\
	&\leq M\nu\left[\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\right)^{\vee}\right]\nonumber\\
&\leq M\mu\left[(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\right]\nonumber\\
&=M\sup\limits_{s\in[-\tau/2,\tau/2]}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|\nonumber\\
	&=M\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|\nonumber\\
	&\leq M\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{ds^{i}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\right)\right|\nonumber\\
	&\hspace*{5cm}\times\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{ds^{m-i}}\left(\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|. \end{align}
Choose $N$ large enough e.g. $N=10m+1$. Then for every $s\in(\alpha-\epsilon,\alpha+\epsilon)$ we have the following estimates:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(i)] $\left|\frac{d^{i}}{ds^{i}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{10m+2}\right)\right|\leq B_{m}|\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s)|^{10m+2-i}$ where $0\leq i\leq m$ and
	\item [(ii)] $\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{ds^{m-i}}\left(\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|\leq C_{m,\phi}/\epsilon^{m-i}.$
\end{enumerate}
The above estimates together with (\ref{eq26}) implies that
\begin{align*}
	\mu\left[(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\right]&\leq M_{m,\phi}\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}|\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s)|^{10m+2-i}\frac{1}{\epsilon^{m-i}}\\
	&\leq D\epsilon^{9m+2}\rightarrow 0\text{ as }\epsilon\rightarrow 0.
\end{align*}
This proves (\ref{eq25}).
Using the same argument given in \cite{KRS2} one can easily prove that  $$(\mathcal{L}-\gamma(\alpha))T_{0}=0.$$
This prove part (a) for radial distribution.
Now we shall prove the result for general case. To avoid triviality, we further assume that $T_{k}$ is nonzero for some (and hence for all) $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.

Observe that for any $L^{2}$-tempered distribution $T$, if $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T)=0$ for every $x\in\mathfrak{X}$ then $T=0$. Indeed the above assumption on $T$ implies that $$\langle\tau_{x}T,\delta_{0}\rangle=T\ast\delta_{0}(x^{-1})=0$$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, where $\delta_{0}$ denotes the Dirac-Delta function at $o$. Since $T\ast\delta_{0}=T$ in the sense of distribution thus $T=0$.
This shows that for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, there exists an $x\in\mathfrak{X}$ such that the distribution $\tau_{x}T_{k}$ has a nonzero radial part.

Now we claim that if $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})\neq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{k})\neq 0$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. To prove this it is enough to show that if $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})\neq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{-1})\neq 0$ and $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{1})\neq 0$.
If $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{-1})=0$ then $\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{-1})=0$. Since $\mathcal L$ commutes with translation and radialization, and  $\mathcal{L}T_{-1}=z_0T_{0}$ for $z_0\neq 0$ thus $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})=0$.
On the other hand if  $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{1})=0$ then $$\langle\tau_{x}T_{1},\phi\rangle=\langle\tau_{x}\mathcal{L}T_{0},\phi\rangle=\langle\tau_{x}T_{0},\mathcal{L}\phi\rangle=0$$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Since $\gamma(s)^{-1}\hat{\psi}(s)\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$.
Thus $\psi$ can be written as $\psi=\mathcal{L}\phi$ for some $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Hence $\tau_{x}T_{0}=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$. This proves our claim.

It is easy to show that for every $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, the sequence $\{\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{k})\}$ of radial distributions satisfies the hypothesis of this theorem.
 Since the result is already proved for radial $L^{2}$-tempered distributions, we have
$$\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})=|z|\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathfrak{X}.$$
Therefore $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}(\mathcal{L}T_{0}-|z|T_{0}))=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{X}$. From above observation we have $\mathcal{L}T_{0}=|z|T_{0}$. This complete the proof of part (a).

We shall prove part (b) of the theorem only for radial case. The proof for the general case follows in a similar way as in part (a). Now assuming that $T_{k}$ are radial, we have for any $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$,

$$	|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|=\left|\left\langle\widehat{T_{k}},\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right\rangle\right|
	\leq M\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right]
	\leq M\mu\left[\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right].$$
If $|z_{0}|<\gamma(s)$ (resp. $|z_{0}|>\gamma(s)$) for $s\in[-\tau/2,\tau/2]$, then letting $k\rightarrow\infty$ (resp. $k\rightarrow -\infty$) in the above equation we conclude that $\langle T_{0},\phi\rangle=0$ for all $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. This completes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma B1
nodes.statement:
We prove the this result for radial distributions, while the general case follows in a similar way as in Theorem \ref{Theorem10}.
For $p\in(1,2)$ let $z_{0}=i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$.  For a fixed $N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ we claim that $$(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}}=0.$$
As observed earlier, for any $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$  we have,
$$ |\langle(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|\leq
M\mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right].$$
Since $\gamma(z)$ and $\phi(z)$ are $\tau-$periodic, even functions on $S_{p}$, so the seminorm $\mu$ on $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ is given by
\begin{align*}
\mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right]&=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\
&=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\
&=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}(z)\text{ (say),}
\end{align*}
where $S_{p}^{+}=\{z\in S_{p}:~\; |\mbox{Re } z|\leq \tau/2\;\; \text{and}\;\;  \Im z\geq 0\}$.

To prove our claim it is enough to show that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$. Now for all $z\in S_{p}^{+}$,
\begin{align}
F_{k}(z)&\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}\right)\right|
\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\nonumber\\
&\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}B_{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}k(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+i-1) \\
&\hspace*{4.8cm}\times\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|.\nonumber
\end{align}
From above inequality we also have
\begin{equation}F_{k}(z)\leq A_{m}k^{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k} \end{equation}

where
$A_{m}=\max\limits_{0\leq i\leq m}\left[\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\right].$

 In the above calculation we have also used the following estimates. For every $z\in S_{p}^{+}$,
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(i)] $\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|\leq 1$,
	\item[(ii)] $\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}\right)\right|\leq B_{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}k(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+i-1)$, where $0\leq i\leq m$.
\end{enumerate}



In order to prove that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$, it is enough to show that
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)]  $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$,
	\item[(b)] $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
\end{enumerate}
 where for $k$ (large enough)
$$V_{k}=\{z\in S_{p}^{+}: |\mbox{Re } z|<(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}\text{ and } \delta_{p}-\log(1+1/k^{1/6})(\log q)^{-1}<\Im z\leq\delta_{p}\}.$$
First we deal with (a). In view of equation (\ref{eq31}), it is sufficient to show that for every $z\in V_{k}^{c}$ there exists a constant $c>0$ such that
\begin{equation} \left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}\leq\left(1+\frac{c}{\sqrt{k}}\right)^{-k}.
\end{equation}

First case, if $0\leq \Im z\leq \delta_{p}-\frac{\log(1+1/k^{1/6})}{\log q}$ then $|\gamma(z)|\geq |\gamma(i(\delta_{p}-\frac{\log(1+1/k^{1/6})}{\log q}))|$.
Hence
\begin{align}
	|\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_{0})|&\geq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)-\left(\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\right)\nonumber\\
	&=\frac{1}{q+1}\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{k^{1/6}(1+k^{1/6})}\left[k^{1/6}(q^{2/p-1}-1)-1\right]. \end{align}
Since $q^{2/p-1}-1>0$, there exists $k_{0}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $k^{1/6}(q^{2/p-1}-1)\geq 2$ for every $k\geq k_{0}$. This together with (\ref{eq33}) gives the desired inequality (\ref{eq32}).

Other case if $z\in V_{k}^{c}$ is such that $\tau/2\geq|\mbox{Re } z|\geq (k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$, then
$$|\gamma(z)|\geq \left(1-\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}cos(k^{-1/4})\right)$$
and
$$|\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_{0})|\geq\left(\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))\right)\geq \frac{c}{k^{1/2}}.$$
Thus for every $z\in V_{k}^{c}$, inequality (\ref{eq32}) holds. Eventually,
$\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.

 Now let us assume that $z\in V_{k}$. Then $z=a+i\delta_{r}$, where $|a|<(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$ and $\delta_{p}-\log(1+1/k^{1/6})(\log q)^{-1}<\delta_{r}\leq\delta_{p}$ and we have
\begin{align*}
	|\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_{0})|^{2}&=\left(\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/r^{\prime}}+q^{1/r}}{q+1}\cos(a\log q)\right)^{2}
	+\left(\frac{q^{1/r}-q^{1/r^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)^{2}\sin^{2}(a\log q)\\
	&\leq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\cos(k^{-1/4})\right)^{2}\\
	&\hspace*{8cm}+\left(\frac{q^{1/p}-q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)^{2}\sin^{2}(k^{-1/4})
\end{align*}
It follows from the inequality $\sqrt{|x|^2+|y|^2}\leq |x|+|y|$ that
\begin{align*}
	|\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_{0})|&\leq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\cos(k^{-1/4})\right)+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\
	&= \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\right)\\
	&\hspace*{3cm}+\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\
	&\leq \frac{c_{3}}{k^{1/6}}+\frac{c_{2}}{k^{1/2}}+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\leq\frac{c}{k^{1/6}},
\end{align*}
where the constants $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ (and hence $c$) are independent of $k$. If we take $N=7m+1$ then each term in equation (\ref{eq30}) atleast contains the factor $(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1-m}=(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{6m+2}$.
Thus from above estimates and equation (\ref{eq30}), we finally have $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\leq \frac{C}{k^{1/3}},$ where $C$ is independent of $k$ and $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.  Using the same argument given in \cite{KRS2} one can easily prove that $N=0$. This completes the proof of part (a) for radial and eventually for general distributions.

The proof of part (b) is similar to that of part (b) Lemma A. To prove part (c), assume that $\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p^{\prime}})>|\lambda|>\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})$. Then $\gamma(S_{p}^{\circ})$ intersects $\{w\in\mathbb C:|w|=|\lambda|\}$ at infinitely many points. Let $p<q<r<2$ be such that $\gamma(\alpha+i\delta_{q^{\prime}})e^{-i\theta_1}=\gamma(\beta+i\delta_{r^{\prime}})e^{-i\theta_2}=\lambda$ for some $\theta_1,\theta_2\in(0,2\pi)$. If we define $T_{k}=e^{ik\theta_1}\phi_{\alpha+i\delta_{q^{\prime}}}+e^{ik\theta_2}\phi_{\beta+i\delta_{r^{\prime}}}$ where $k\in\mathbb Z_{+}$, then $T_k$ satisfies all the hypothesis of Lemma B1 but $T_0$ fails to be an eigen-distribution of $\mathcal L$.

nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$
nodes.statement_short: Using only positive powers in Theorem A fails: a sum of two spherical functions with smaller eigenvalues is a counterexample.

nodes.name: Theorem B fails off the special points
nodes.statement: The conclusions of Theorem B, Part $1$ (resp. Part $2$) does not hold for $z=\alpha\pm i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$ where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus (n\tau)\mathbb{Z}$ (resp. $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus ((2n+1)\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$). The counterexamples can be constructed in a similar way as we did in Lemma B1, part (c).
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$

nodes.name: other Lorentz norms admit non-eigenfunctions
nodes.statement: In Theorem B (resp. in Theorem A), if we consider $z=\alpha\pm i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$ where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ (resp. $z\in\mathbb R$) and substitute the $L^{p^{\prime},\infty}$ norm (resp. $L^{2,\infty}$) by the $L^{q^{\prime},r}$ where $1\leq q<p<2$ (resp. $L^{p^{\prime},r}$ where $1<p<2$, $1\leq r\leq\infty$ or $L^{\infty}$), then there are functions which satisfies the hypothesis but are not eigenfunctions of $\mathcal L$.
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$

nodes.name: Laplace operator on Z
nodes.statement:
The Laplace operator on $\mathbb{Z}$ is defined as
$$\mathcal L_{\mathbb{Z}} f(m)=f(m)-\frac{f(m-1)+f(m+1)}{2}\quad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}.$$

nodes.name: Fourier transform on Z
nodes.statement:
The Fourier transform $\widehat{f}$ of a finitely supported function $f$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}$, is a function on $\mathbb{T}$ given by
$$\widehat{f}(s)=\sum\limits_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}f(m)e^{ims}\quad\text{ where }f(m)=\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi}\widehat{f}(s)e^{ims}ds$$
represents it's inverse Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Schwartz space on Z
nodes.statement: Let us define the Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})=\{f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}:\lambda_{n}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }n\in\mathbb{N}\}$, equipped with the countable family of semi-norms $\lambda_{n}(f)=\sup(1+|m|)^{n}|f(m)|$.

nodes.name: Fourier isomorphism on Z
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that the map $f\rightarrow\widehat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ onto $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)$ where $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)=\{g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}:g\text{ is infintely differentiable on }\mathbb{R},~g(x+\pi)=g(x)\text{ and }\mu_{l}(g)<\infty\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R},l\in\mathbb{N}\text{ respectively}\}$ where $\mu_{l}(g)=\sup|g^{(l)}(s)|$ defines a countable family of semi-norms.
conclusions: the map $f\rightarrow\widehat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ onto $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)$
nodes.statement_short: The Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal S(\mathbb Z)$ onto smooth periodic functions $\mathcal C^\infty(\mathbb T)$.

nodes.name: distribution on Z and its Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
Analogous to the Euclidean case, a distribution $T$ is a continuous linear functional on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ whose Fourier transform is defined as
$$\langle \widehat{T},\phi\rangle=\langle T,\left(\phi^{\vee}\right)^{\#}\rangle,\text{ where }\widehat{\phi^{\vee}}=\phi\text{ and }\left(\phi^{\vee}\right)^{\#}(m)=\phi^{\vee}(-m).$$

nodes.name: Proof pointer for the theorem on Z
nodes.statement: Now we state the Theorem  on $\mathbb{Z}$, which  can be proved by the similar argument developed by Roe in \cite{R}.
nodes.statement_short: Follows Roe's original argument.

nodes.name: Roe's theorem on Z
nodes.statement:
Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinte sequence of functions on $\mathbb{Z}$ which satisfies
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{Z}} f_{k}=(1-\cos\alpha)f_{k+1}\quad\text{ for }\alpha\neq 0$
	and there exists constants $M_{k}\geq 0$, $\beta\in(0,1]$ and a non-negative integer $n$ such that
	$|f_{k}(m)|\leq M_{k}(1+|m|)^{n+\beta}\text{ for all }k,m\in\mathbb{Z}.$	
If $\liminf\limits_{k\rightarrow \infty}\frac{M_{k}}{(1+\epsilon)^{k}}=0$  and $\liminf\limits_{k\rightarrow \infty}\frac{M_{-k}}{(1+\epsilon)^{k}}=0$  for all $ \epsilon>0$ 	then $f_{0}(m)=p(m)e^{im\alpha}+q(m)e^{-im\alpha}$ where $p,q$ are polynomials of degree atmost $n$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathbb Z$, if $\mathcal L_{\mathbb Z}f_k=(1-\cos\alpha)f_{k+1}$ with polynomially bounded $f_k$ of subexponential constants, then $f_0$ is a polynomial-modulated exponential $e^{\pm im\alpha}$.
assumptions:
$\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinte sequence of functions on $\mathbb{Z}$ which satisfies
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{Z}} f_{k}=(1-\cos\alpha)f_{k+1}\quad\text{ for }\alpha\neq 0$

there exists constants $M_{k}\geq 0$, $\beta\in(0,1]$ and a non-negative integer $n$ such that
	$|f_{k}(m)|\leq M_{k}(1+|m|)^{n+\beta}\text{ for all }k,m\in\mathbb{Z}.$
conclusions: $f_{0}(m)=p(m)e^{im\alpha}+q(m)e^{-im\alpha}$ where $p,q$ are polynomials of degree atmost $n$
nodes.label: Theorem4.1

nodes.name: extension to Z^n
nodes.statement:
\noindent Remark:
	We can also extend the above result to $\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ (as done by Strichartz \cite{S}) where the Laplacian is defined as
	$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}f(m)=f(m)-\frac{1}{2n}\sum\limits_{k:|m-k|=1}f(k).$$
But here we assume that $M_{k}$ satisfies a sublinear growth, that is $\lim\limits_{k\rightarrow \pm\infty}\frac{M_{k}}{k}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The result extends to $\mathbb Z^n$ (as Strichartz did for $\mathbb R^n$) assuming sublinear growth of $M_k$.

nodes.name: Abel transform form of the spherical transform
nodes.statement:
Recalling expression (\ref{Equation 2.6}), the spherical Fourier transform of a function $f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ can also be written as
\begin{equation} \hat{f}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz},
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{A}f$ denotes the Abel transformation of $f$.

nodes.name: spherical transform via Abel transform (eq15)
nodes.statement: \hat{f}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz},
nodes.label: eq15

nodes.name: Abel transform isomorphism (Cowling-Meda-Setti)
nodes.statement_short: The Abel transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal S_p(\mathfrak X)^\#$ onto $q^{-\delta_p|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb Z)$, with explicit seminorm comparisons.
conclusions: $f\rightarrow\mathcal{A}f$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$

nodes.name: seminorm comparison (eq16)
nodes.statement: C^{-1}\lambda_{(m-2)}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}\mathcal{A}f)\leq\nu_{m}(f)\leq C\lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}\mathcal{A}f).
nodes.label: eq16

nodes.name: isomorphism theorem for the spherical Fourier transform on S_p
nodes.statement: The map $f\rightarrow\hat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$, for every $p\in(1,2]$.
conclusions: The map $f\rightarrow\hat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$
nodes.label: lp isom

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement:
Fix $p\in(1,2)$ (proof of the case $p=2$ is similar). Let $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ and $z\in S_p$. Then it is clear that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on $S_p$ and consequently $\hat{f}$ is well-defined. The analyticity of $\hat{f}$ on $S_p^{\circ}$ follows directly from the analyticity of $q^{inz}$ together with the fact that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on any compact subset of $S_p^{o}$. Infact for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$,
$$\hat{f}^{(m)}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(in\log q)^m\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz},\quad\text{for all } z\in S_p^{o}.$$
The above expression together with equation (\ref{eq16}) implies that for every semi-norm $\mu_{m}$ of $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$, there exists a semi-norm $\nu_{(m+4)}$ of $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that,
$$\mu_{m}(\hat{f})\leq C\nu_{(m+4)}(f)\quad\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}.$$
Conversely, assume $g\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$. Then for all $r$ with $p<r\leq 2$, the function $g(\cdot+i\delta_{r})$ is an infinitely differentiable function of period $\tau$. Hence g has a Fourier series representation of the form $g(s)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}F(n)q^{ins}$, where
$$F(n)=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s)q^{-ins}ds$$
yields the $n^{\text{th}}$ Fourier co-efficient of the function $g$. Our aim is to prove that $F\in q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$. Applying the Cauchy's integral theorem to $g$, it is easy to verify that for every $r\in(p,2]$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$,
\begin{align}
F(n)&=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s+i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s+i\delta_{r})}ds=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s-i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s-i\delta_{r})}ds. \end{align}
Infact the first equality in (\ref{eq19}) can be proved using the closed rectangle
\begin{multline*}
\Gamma(z)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=0,-\tau/2\leq \mbox{Re } z\leq\tau/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}: \mbox{Re } z=\tau/2,0\leq \Im z\leq\delta_{r}\}\\
\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=\delta_{r},\tau/2\leq \mbox{Re } z\leq-\tau/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\mbox{Re } z=-\tau/2,\delta_{r}\leq \Im z\leq 0\}.
\end{multline*}
Using the identities (\ref{eq19}) and noting that $g$ is even, one can easily prove that $F(-n)=F(n)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, that $F$ is even in $\mathbb{Z}$. Integrating by parts the second equation in (\ref{eq19}) (m times) and further using the Dominated convergence theorem and letting $r\rightarrow p$ we have,
\begin{equation} \lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}F)\leq C \mu_{m}(g)\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.
\end{equation}
Hence there exists an unique $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that $\mathcal{A}f=F$ and $g=\hat{f}$. Further using equations (\ref{eq16}) and (\ref{eq21}) we conclude that
$$\nu_{m}(f)\leq C \mu_{m}(\hat{f})\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.$$
This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\hat f$ as a Fourier series in the Abel transform and transfer seminorm bounds; conversely recover $\mathcal Af$ from Fourier coefficients shifted by Cauchy's theorem.

nodes.name: shifted Fourier coefficients (eq19)
nodes.statement: F(n)&=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s+i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s+i\delta_{r})}ds=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s-i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s-i\delta_{r})}ds.
nodes.label: eq19

nodes.name: seminorm bound for F (eq21)
nodes.statement: \lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}F)\leq C \mu_{m}(g)\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.
nodes.label: eq21

nodes.name: parametrize z0
nodes.statement: Fix $z_{0}\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z_{0}|\in[1-b,1+b]$. Then $z_{0}=\gamma(\alpha)e^{i\theta}$ for a unique $\alpha\in[0,\tau/2]$ where $\theta=\arg z_{0}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Write $z_0=\gamma(\alpha)e^{i\theta}$ with $\alpha\in[0,\tau/2]$

nodes.name: Fourier-side relation
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Iterate hypothesis (1) and pass to spherical transforms (eq23)

nodes.name: pairing with test functions away from alpha
nodes.statement:
Let $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ be such that $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\tau/2,-\alpha-r]\cup[\alpha+r,\tau/2]$ where $r>0$. Observing the fact that $\gamma(\alpha)^{k}/\gamma(\cdot)^{k}\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ and using hypothesis (2) of the theorem, we have

$$|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|=\left|\left\langle\widehat{T_{k}},e^{ik\theta}\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right\rangle\right|=\left|\left\langle T_{k},\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right\rangle\right|
	\leq M\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right].$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Bound the pairing with test functions supported away from $\pm\alpha$ via hypothesis (2)

nodes.name: seminorm decay
nodes.statement:
By the isomorphism theorem \ref{lp isom}, there exists  a fixed seminorm $\mu$ on $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ such that
$$\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right]
	\leq C\mu\left[\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(\cdot)}\right)^{k}\phi\right]=\sup\limits_{\alpha+r\leq|s|\leq\tau/2}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(\alpha)}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)\right|\rightarrow 0\text{ as }k\rightarrow\infty.$$
 By similar argument as above and letting $k\rightarrow -\infty$, we can show that $\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle=0$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\alpha+r,\alpha-r]$. We proved that for any $r>0$ and for every $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ such that $\mbox{supp}(\phi)\subseteq[-\tau/2,-\alpha-r]\cup[-\alpha+r,\alpha-r]\cup[\alpha+r,\tau/2]$, $\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Use the isomorphism theorem to show the bound tends to 0, so $\widehat{T_0}$ is supported at $\pm\alpha$

nodes.name: claim: generalized eigen-relation
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Claim $(\mathcal L-\gamma(\alpha))^{N+1}T_0=0$, reduced to the Fourier side

nodes.name: reduce to Fourier side
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: By the isomorphism, it suffices to prove (eq25)

nodes.name: cutoff psi_epsilon
nodes.statement:
Let $g$ be an infinitely differentiable even function on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $g\equiv 1$ on $[-1/2,1/2]$ and $\mbox{supp}(g)\subseteq(-1,1)$. Define
$$\psi_{\epsilon}(s)=\begin{cases}
g((s-\alpha)/\epsilon) & s\in[0,\tau/2]\\
g((-s-\alpha)/\epsilon) & s\in[-\tau/2,0].
\end{cases}
$$
Here $\epsilon$ is suitably chosen positive number such that $\psi_{\epsilon}\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with $\mbox{supp}(\psi_{\epsilon})\subseteq(-\alpha-\epsilon,-\alpha+\epsilon)\cup(\alpha-\epsilon,\alpha+\epsilon)$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Construct the even cutoff $\psi_\epsilon$ around $\pm\alpha$

nodes.name: localize with the cutoff
nodes.statement:
Note that if $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$, then $(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(\cdot))^{N+1}\phi(1-\psi_{\epsilon})\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ with its support inside $[-\tau/2,-\alpha-\epsilon/2]\cup[-\alpha+\epsilon/2,\alpha-\epsilon/2]\cup[\alpha+\epsilon/2,\tau/2]$. and using the result proved in step 1, we have
\begin{align}
	|\langle(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|	 &\leq|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(1-\psi_{\epsilon})\rangle|+|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\rangle|\nonumber\\
	&=|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\rangle|\nonumber\\
	&\leq M\nu\left[\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\right)^{\vee}\right]\nonumber\\
&\leq M\mu\left[(\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi\psi_{\epsilon}\right]\nonumber\\
&=M\sup\limits_{s\in[-\tau/2,\tau/2]}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|\nonumber\\
	&=M\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{ds^{m}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|\nonumber\\
	&\leq M\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{ds^{i}}\left((\gamma(\alpha)-\gamma(s))^{N+1}\right)\right|\nonumber\\
	&\hspace*{5cm}\times\sup\limits_{\alpha-\epsilon\leq |s|\leq\alpha+\epsilon}\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{ds^{m-i}}\left(\phi(s)\psi_{\epsilon}(s)\right)\right|. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Split the test function with $\psi_\epsilon$ and bound the remaining term (eq26)

nodes.statement:
Using the same argument given in \cite{KRS2} one can easily prove that  $$(\mathcal{L}-\gamma(\alpha))T_{0}=0.$$
This prove part (a) for radial distribution.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $N=0$ as in KRS2, proving part (a) for radial distributions

nodes.name: general case setup
nodes.statement: Now we shall prove the result for general case. To avoid triviality, we further assume that $T_{k}$ is nonzero for some (and hence for all) $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Turn to the general case, assuming the $T_k$ nonzero

nodes.name: radial parts detect nonzero distributions
nodes.statement:
Observe that for any $L^{2}$-tempered distribution $T$, if $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T)=0$ for every $x\in\mathfrak{X}$ then $T=0$. Indeed the above assumption on $T$ implies that $$\langle\tau_{x}T,\delta_{0}\rangle=T\ast\delta_{0}(x^{-1})=0$$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, where $\delta_{0}$ denotes the Dirac-Delta function at $o$. Since $T\ast\delta_{0}=T$ in the sense of distribution thus $T=0$.
This shows that for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, there exists an $x\in\mathfrak{X}$ such that the distribution $\tau_{x}T_{k}$ has a nonzero radial part.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: A distribution all of whose translated radial parts vanish is zero

nodes.name: claim: nonvanishing radial part propagates
nodes.statement:
Now we claim that if $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})
eq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{k})
eq 0$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. To prove this it is enough to show that if $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})
eq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})
eq 0$ and $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{1})
eq 0$.
If $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})=0$ then $\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})=0$. Since $\mathcal L$ commutes with translation and radialization, and  $\mathcal{L}T_{-1}=z_0T_{0}$ for $z_0
eq 0$ thus $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})=0$.
On the other hand if  $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{1})=0$ then $$\langle	au_{x}T_{1},\phiangle=\langle	au_{x}\mathcal{L}T_{0},\phiangle=\langle	au_{x}T_{0},\mathcal{L}\phiangle=0$$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Since $\gamma(s)^{-1}\hat{\psi}(s)\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$.
Thus $\psi$ can be written as $\psi=\mathcal{L}\phi$ for some $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Hence $	au_{x}T_{0}=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$. This proves our claim.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Claim a nonzero translated radial part of $T_0$ gives nonzero ones for every $T_k$

nodes.name: reduce to neighbours
nodes.statement:
To prove this it is enough to show that if $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{0})
eq 0$ for some $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, then $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{-1})
eq 0$ and $\varepsilon(	au_{x}T_{1})
eq 0$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to treat $T_{-1}$ and $T_1$

nodes.name: case T_{-1}
nodes.statement: If $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{-1})=0$ then $\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{-1})=0$. Since $\mathcal L$ commutes with translation and radialization, and  $\mathcal{L}T_{-1}=z_0T_{0}$ for $z_0\neq 0$ thus $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: If the radial part of $T_{-1}$ vanishes, so does that of $T_0$

nodes.name: case T_1
nodes.statement:
On the other hand if  $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{1})=0$ then $$\langle\tau_{x}T_{1},\phi\rangle=\langle\tau_{x}\mathcal{L}T_{0},\phi\rangle=\langle\tau_{x}T_{0},\mathcal{L}\phi\rangle=0$$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Since $\gamma(s)^{-1}\hat{\psi}(s)\in\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$.
Thus $\psi$ can be written as $\psi=\mathcal{L}\phi$ for some $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. Hence $\tau_{x}T_{0}=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak X$. This proves our claim.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: If the radial part of $T_1$ vanishes, invert $\mathcal L$ on test functions to get $\tau_xT_0=0$

nodes.name: apply the radial case
nodes.statement:
It is easy to show that for every $x\in\mathfrak{X}$, the sequence $\{\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{k})\}$ of radial distributions satisfies the hypothesis of this theorem.
 Since the result is already proved for radial $L^{2}$-tempered distributions, we have
$$\mathcal{L}\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})=|z|\varepsilon(\tau_{x}T_{0})\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathfrak{X}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Apply the radial case to the translated radialized sequence

nodes.name: conclude part (a)
nodes.statement: Therefore $\varepsilon(\tau_{x}(\mathcal{L}T_{0}-|z|T_{0}))=0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak{X}$. From above observation we have $\mathcal{L}T_{0}=|z|T_{0}$. This complete the proof of part (a).
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $\mathcal LT_0=|z|T_0$ by the observation

nodes.name: part (b) setup
nodes.statement: We shall prove part (b) of the theorem only for radial case. The proof for the general case follows in a similar way as in part (a).
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Prove part (b) only in the radial case

nodes.name: bound for part (b)
nodes.statement:
Now assuming that $T_{k}$ are radial, we have for any $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$,

$$	|\langle\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|=\left|\left\langle\widehat{T_{k}},\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right\rangle\right|
	\leq M\nu\left[\left(\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right)^{\vee}\right]
	\leq M\mu\left[\left(\frac{z_{0}}{\gamma(s)}\right)^{k}\phi\right].$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Bound the pairing by $\mu[(z_0/\gamma)^k\phi]$

nodes.name: let k tend to infinity
nodes.statement: If $|z_{0}|<\gamma(s)$ (resp. $|z_{0}|>\gamma(s)$) for $s\in[-\tau/2,\tau/2]$, then letting $k\rightarrow\infty$ (resp. $k\rightarrow -\infty$) in the above equation we conclude that $\langle T_{0},\phi\rangle=0$ for all $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Let $k\to\pm\infty$ to get $T_0=0$

nodes.name: reduce to radial
nodes.statement: We prove the this result for radial distributions, while the general case follows in a similar way as in Theorem \ref{Theorem10}.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Prove for radial distributions; general case as in Lemma A

nodes.name: claim on Fourier side
nodes.statement: For $p\in(1,2)$ let $z_{0}=i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$.  For a fixed $N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ we claim that $$(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}}=0.$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Set $z_0=i\delta_{p'}$ and claim $(\gamma(z_0)-\gamma)^{N+1}\widehat{T_0}=0$

nodes.name: seminorm bound
nodes.statement:
As observed earlier, for any $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$  we have,
$$ |\langle(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|\leq
M\mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right].$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Bound the pairing by a holomorphic seminorm $\mu$

nodes.name: reduce to S_p^+
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: By evenness and periodicity reduce the sup to $S_p^+$, defining $F_k$

nodes.name: goal sup F_k to 0
nodes.statement: To prove our claim it is enough to show that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show $\sup F_k\to0$

nodes.name: Leibniz bound
nodes.statement:
Now for all $z\in S_{p}^{+}$,
\begin{align}
F_{k}(z)&\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}\right)\right|
\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\nonumber\\
&\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}B_{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}k(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+i-1) \\
&\hspace*{4.8cm}\times\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|.\nonumber
\end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Leibniz rule bound (eq30)

nodes.name: polynomial times geometric bound
nodes.statement:
From above inequality we also have
\begin{equation}F_{k}(z)\leq A_{m}k^{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k} \end{equation}

where
$A_{m}=\max\limits_{0\leq i\leq m}\left[\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\right].$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Deduce $F_k\le A_mk^m|\gamma(z_0)/\gamma(z)|^k$ (eq31)

nodes.name: auxiliary estimates
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Record the estimates used: ratio at most 1 and derivative bounds

nodes.name: split by V_k
nodes.statement:
In order to prove that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$, it is enough to show that
\begin{enumerate}
	\item[(a)]  $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$,
	\item[(b)] $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
\end{enumerate}
 where for $k$ (large enough)
$$V_{k}=\{z\in S_{p}^{+}: |\mbox{Re } z|<(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}\text{ and } \delta_{p}-\log(1+1/k^{1/6})(\log q)^{-1}<\Im z\leq\delta_{p}\}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Split $S_p^+$ into $V_k$ and its complement

nodes.name: reduce (a) to eq32
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: On $V_k^c$ it suffices to prove (eq32)

nodes.name: imaginary part away from delta_p
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Case of small imaginary part: gap estimate (eq33) gives (eq32)

nodes.name: real part away from 0
nodes.statement:
Other case if $z\in V_{k}^{c}$ is such that $\tau/2\geq|\mbox{Re } z|\geq (k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$, then
$$|\gamma(z)|\geq \left(1-\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}cos(k^{-1/4})\right)$$
and
$$|\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_{0})|\geq\left(\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))\right)\geq \frac{c}{k^{1/2}}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Case of large real part: cosine gap gives (eq32)

nodes.name: conclude (a)
nodes.statement:
Thus for every $z\in V_{k}^{c}$, inequality (\ref{eq32}) holds. Eventually,
$\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\sup_{V_k^c}F_k\to0$

nodes.name: z in V_k
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: For $z\in V_k$ expand $|\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_0)|^2$

nodes.name: gap at most c/k^{1/6}
nodes.statement:
It follows from the inequality $\sqrt{|x|^2+|y|^2}\leq |x|+|y|$ that
\begin{align*}
	|\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_{0})|&\leq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\cos(k^{-1/4})\right)+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\
	&= \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\right)\\
	&\hspace*{3cm}+\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\
	&\leq \frac{c_{3}}{k^{1/6}}+\frac{c_{2}}{k^{1/2}}+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\leq\frac{c}{k^{1/6}},
\end{align*}
where the constants $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ (and hence $c$) are independent of $k$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_0)|\le c/k^{1/6}$

nodes.name: choose N
nodes.statement: If we take $N=7m+1$ then each term in equation (\ref{eq30}) atleast contains the factor $(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1-m}=(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{6m+2}$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: With $N=7m+1$ each term carries a high power of $\gamma(z_0)-\gamma(z)$

nodes.name: conclude sup F_k to 0
nodes.statement: Thus from above estimates and equation (\ref{eq30}), we finally have $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\leq \frac{C}{k^{1/3}},$ where $C$ is independent of $k$ and $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Get $\sup_{V_k}F_k\le C/k^{1/3}$, so $\sup F_k\to0$

nodes.name: reduce N to zero
nodes.statement: Using the same argument given in \cite{KRS2} one can easily prove that $N=0$. This completes the proof of part (a) for radial and eventually for general distributions.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $N=0$ as in KRS2, completing part (a)

nodes.name: part (b)
nodes.statement: The proof of part (b) is similar to that of part (b) Lemma A.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Part (b) as in Lemma A

nodes.name: part (c) setup
nodes.statement: To prove part (c), assume that $\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p^{\prime}})>|\lambda|>\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})$. Then $\gamma(S_{p}^{\circ})$ intersects $\{w\in\mathbb C:|w|=|\lambda|\}$ at infinitely many points.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: In the intermediate range the circle $|w|=|\lambda|$ meets $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ infinitely often

nodes.name: counterexample construction
nodes.statement: Let $p<q<r<2$ be such that $\gamma(\alpha+i\delta_{q^{\prime}})e^{-i\theta_1}=\gamma(\beta+i\delta_{r^{\prime}})e^{-i\theta_2}=\lambda$ for some $\theta_1,\theta_2\in(0,2\pi)$. If we define $T_{k}=e^{ik\theta_1}\phi_{\alpha+i\delta_{q^{\prime}}}+e^{ik\theta_2}\phi_{\beta+i\delta_{r^{\prime}}}$ where $k\in\mathbb Z_{+}$, then $T_k$ satisfies all the hypothesis of Lemma B1 but $T_0$ fails to be an eigen-distribution of $\mathcal L$.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Sum of two spherical functions gives a non-eigen solution

nodes.name: Theorem A from Lemma A
nodes.statement: Now we will conclude the rest of the proof of the our main theorems. Let $z_0=\gamma(z)$ for $z\in\mathbb R\setminus\tau/2\mathbb Z$. From the give assumption in Theorem A if we define $T_k=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal L^k f$ then $T_k$ is a $L^2$-tempered distribution and the proof of the Theorem A is a consequence of the Lemma A.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Set $T_k=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal L^kf$ and apply Lemma A

nodes.name: Theorem B part 1 from Lemma B1
nodes.statement: Similarly if we assume that $T_{k}=\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})^{-k}\mathcal{L}^{k}f$ where $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$. According to the hypothesis of Theorem B, $\|T_{k}\|_{p^\prime,\infty}\leq M$	 for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$. It is easy to show that each $T_{k}$ is an $L^p$-tempered distribution which satisfies all the hypothesis of Lemma B1. Hence $\mathcal{L}f=\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})f$. This completes the proof of the 1st part of Theorem B.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Same normalization with $\gamma(i\delta_{p'})$ and apply Lemma B1

nodes.name: Theorem B part 2 from Lemma B2
nodes.statement: The remaining part of Theorem B will follow from  the Lemma B2.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B
nodes.statement_short: Part 2 of Theorem B from Lemma B2

nodes.name: fix p and f
nodes.statement: Fix $p\in(1,2)$ (proof of the case $p=2$ is similar). Let $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ and $z\in S_p$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $p$, $f$ and $z$

nodes.name: well-definedness
nodes.statement: Then it is clear that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on $S_p$ and consequently $\hat{f}$ is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: The Abel-series for $\hat f$ converges uniformly

nodes.name: analyticity and derivatives
nodes.statement:
The analyticity of $\hat{f}$ on $S_p^{\circ}$ follows directly from the analyticity of $q^{inz}$ together with the fact that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on any compact subset of $S_p^{o}$. Infact for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$,
$$\hat{f}^{(m)}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(in\log q)^m\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz},\quad\text{for all } z\in S_p^{o}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Holomorphy on $S_p^\circ$ with termwise derivatives

nodes.name: continuity of f to hat f
nodes.statement:
The above expression together with equation (\ref{eq16}) implies that for every semi-norm $\mu_{m}$ of $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$, there exists a semi-norm $\nu_{(m+4)}$ of $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that,
$$\mu_{m}(\hat{f})\leq C\nu_{(m+4)}(f)\quad\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Seminorm bound $\mu_m(\hat f)\le C\nu_{m+4}(f)$

nodes.name: Fourier series of g
nodes.statement:
Conversely, assume $g\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$. Then for all $r$ with $p<r\leq 2$, the function $g(\cdot+i\delta_{r})$ is an infinitely differentiable function of period $\tau$. Hence g has a Fourier series representation of the form $g(s)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}F(n)q^{ins}$, where
$$F(n)=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s)q^{-ins}ds$$
yields the $n^{\text{th}}$ Fourier co-efficient of the function $g$.
nodes.statement_short: For $g\in\mathcal H(S_p)^\#$ take its Fourier coefficients $F(n)$

nodes.name: goal
nodes.statement: Our aim is to prove that $F\in q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$.
nodes.statement_short: Aim: $F\in q^{-\delta_p|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb Z)$

nodes.name: shift contour
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's theorem shifts the coefficient integral to $\Im s=\pm\delta_r$ (eq19)

nodes.name: evenness of F
nodes.statement: Using the identities (\ref{eq19}) and noting that $g$ is even, one can easily prove that $F(-n)=F(n)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, that $F$ is even in $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is even

nodes.name: decay of F
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts and $r\to p$ give (eq21)

nodes.name: inverse map
nodes.statement:
Hence there exists an unique $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that $\mathcal{A}f=F$ and $g=\hat{f}$. Further using equations (\ref{eq16}) and (\ref{eq21}) we conclude that
$$\nu_{m}(f)\leq C \mu_{m}(\hat{f})\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.$$
This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Invert via the Abel isomorphism and get the reverse seminorm bound
